| Alpha, example | $25 per day | Standard setup example | [L0225.027] |
| Same for both campaigns | $15 or about $20 per day each | Course build with Alpha and Beta at equal budget | [L0746.025] |
| Alpha and beta, each | $20 per day each | Narrow starter feed of about 20 products | [L0470.027] |
| Each campaign | $10-$30 per day | New store with 500+ products, two-week data window | [L0270.056] |
| Alpha, 2019 | $30 per day | Older setup | [L0243.033] |
| Beta, 2019 | $17 per day | Older setup | [L0243.034] |
| Example of imbalanced spend | Alpha $100/day, Beta $8/day | Shared budget with proper priority to allocate spend | [L0274.013] |

- *(Older advice, 2019)* Set Alpha to a higher daily budget (e.g., $30) and Beta to a lower one (e.g., $17). [L0243.033, L0243.034]
- *(Older advice, 2020)* Alpha: set the budget higher. Beta: set it lower. [L0243.033]
- *(Older advice, 2021)* Let all campaigns run with $10-$30 per day. [L0270.056]
- *(Older advice, 2023)* With a daily budget of 20 USD for each alpha and beta campaign, start with a narrow feed of about 20 products rather than a large catalog of around 1,000. [L0470.027]
- *(Older advice, 2023)* If Alpha spends $100 a day and Beta spends $8 a day, set up a shared budget with the correct priority (Alpha high, Beta low). Note that this example reverses the priority of the standard alpha-beta setup. [L0274.013]

#### Shared Budget Pairs (Older, 2024)

- *(Older advice, 2024)* One shared budget is associated with two campaigns, such as alpha and beta bestsellers. A second shared budget is associated with the alpha and beta everything-else campaigns. [L0360.036]
- *(Older advice, 2024)* Shopping campaigns are built as pairs of an alpha and beta campaign for each product group, such as alpha bestsellers and beta bestsellers. Each pair is attached to one shared budget. Separate pairs are set up for each country or region served. [L0360.090]

### Networks, Location and Dates

#### Networks

| Setting | Recommendation | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Google Search Partners | Off. Conversion rates are better on Google itself. Networks field should read "no networks targeted". | [L0186.006, L0186.007, L0743.017, L0746.025] |
| Google Search Partners | On by default in one course unit; this conflicts with the rest of the course (no date given) | [L0225.020] |
| YouTube, Gmail, Discover | Include (older, 2021-2022) | [L0742.012] |
| YouTube, Gmail, Discover | Uncheck; ads run only on google.com, which is where the campaign is meant to show | [L0746.017, L0746.025] |

- Turn off Google Search Partners under the Networks setting. It is on by default, and its placements convert much worse. The Networks field should then read "no networks targeted". [L0743.017]
- Find the Networks setting (very important; may be under "More settings") and turn Include Google Search Partners off. Conversion rates on Google Shopping are best on Google itself, not on Search Partners. [L0186.006]
- Leave Google search partners on by default. These include Google Maps and websites with search boxes. You can analyze their performance separately later, but they generally perform similarly to Google Search. *(No year given; this conflicts with the advice to turn search partners off.)* [L0225.020]
- *(Older advice, 2021-2022)* Keep the Search Network. Do not include Google search partners, because their performance cannot be tracked, sites cannot be excluded and search terms are not visible. Include YouTube, Gmail and Discover, because Shopping ads perform well there with strong evidence. [L0742.012]
- For Shopping campaigns, keep the Google search network and uncheck Include search partners, as well as YouTube, Gmail and Discover. With these unchecked, ads run only on google.com. Set the location to one country per campaign. [L0746.017]

#### Location

- Location targeting defaults to the country of the Merchant Center feed and the Google Ads account. For multi-country selling, use separate feeds per country. Prices must be shown in the local currency as a Merchant Center requirement. *(Older advice, 2021-2022)* [L0742.014]
- The location step asks for each country where ads should show. Europe-wide ads require selecting every EU country in the list. Countries can also be chosen individually, such as only Spain and Italy. The same location settings appear when setting up Meta campaigns. *(Older advice, 2024)* [L0360.029]
- For the broad Beta campaign, leave the location on the country where the business sells. In this setup that was the United States. [L0743.028]
- Select the country (e.g., United States) and set devices to All devices. [L0225.027]
- Set the location to one country per campaign. [L0746.017]

#### Dates and Ad Group Type

- Start date: the date the campaign is created. No end date is set. *(Older advice, 2021-2022)* [L0742.015]
- Set the start date to as soon as possible and leave the end date empty, so the campaign runs indefinitely. [L0746.022]
- Keep the ad group type on Product shopping, which is the default. Do not use Showcase shopping. [L0746.022]
- For the first ad group, choose the ad group type Product Shopping with Create single product ads rather than Showcase Shopping. Product Shopping ads show the product image and send the shopper straight to the product to buy it. *(Older advice, 2021-2022)* [L0742.039]

### Campaign Priority and the Alpha-Beta Logic

#### Priority Rules

- Campaign priorities (high, medium, low) apply only between your own campaigns, not against competitors. Google checks high priority first, then medium, then low, for each search query across your account. [L0225.008]
- Google checks higher-priority campaigns first. Beta is set to High so that broad searches are checked first. Alpha is set to Low so that searches not blocked by Beta fall through to it. This is counterintuitive, because Beta is the less valuable campaign. [L0746.006]
- Set the Beta campaign to High priority and keep Alpha on Low (the default). [L0743.007]
- In a new Shopping campaign, the Campaign priority field defaults to Low. Beta must be changed to High, while Alpha stays at Low, so the intended order of checking takes effect. [L0746.034]
- Set the alpha campaign to low priority so Google checks it second, and the beta campaign to high priority so Google checks it first. When a search matches negatives in the high-priority beta campaign, it funnels to the low-priority alpha campaign. [L0225.007]
- Set your alpha campaign priority to low and your beta campaign priority to high. This counterintuitive setting ensures beta (low-converting) terms are checked first. When blocked by negatives, traffic funnels to alpha (high-converting) terms at the correct priority level. [L0225.023]
- *(Older advice, 2019)* Set the campaign priority to Low for Alpha and High for Beta. Google checks the High-priority campaign first for matching searches. [L0243.033, L0243.034]

#### Alpha-Beta Logic

- *(Older advice, 2019)* When a search query matches both campaigns, Google checks Beta first, because it has higher priority. If the query is blocked as a negative in Beta, Google moves to Alpha. If the query matches Alpha and is not blocked there, the ad shows with Alpha's higher bid. This prevents budget waste on weak keywords by reserving high-bid spend for strong keywords. [L0243.035]
- Negative keywords in Beta push searches for high-converting terms into Alpha. Beta is checked first as high priority and blocks the negatives. Alpha, on low priority, picks up the same searches at its higher bid. [L0743.026]
- Negative keywords in the Beta campaign act as a filter. When a search matches one of them, Google skips Beta and passes the search to the lower-priority Alpha campaign. Beta negatives should be the terms most relevant to the store's own products: brand names, SKU numbers and popular product names, which are the searches Alpha should win. [L0746.008]
- The inverted priority structure forces budget toward high-converting searches. This blocks those searches in the high-priority Beta campaign, so Google routes them to Alpha, where you bid higher. [L0186.005]
- Priority of the alpha-beta structure: Beta, High, checked first; Alpha, Low, checked second. [L0225.007, L0746.006]
- Alpha holds the high-traffic campaigns and blocks weak search terms with negative keywords. Beta holds the keywords that still convert but are weaker. [L0671.011, L0671.289]
- Always keep a separate alpha and beta split in Shopping campaigns. If only an "all brands" beta campaign exists with no alpha campaign, the setup is incorrect and must be configured properly. [L0745.011]
- Every product not explicitly filtered is caught by a catch-all product group at each level. Check your product group inheritance structure carefully so products you intended to separate are not grouped together by accident. [L0225.011]

### Campaign Roles: Alpha and Beta

#### Alpha

- Alpha campaigns target high-converting, branded or commercial terms, with aggressive bidding to maximize revenue and visibility. Use negative keywords to block weak or generic terms from appearing in alpha campaigns. [L0225.002]
- Alpha targets high-intent searches: brand names, product names, and SKU/MPN numbers. [L0186.004, L0186.003]
- Alpha campaigns hold the high-traffic campaigns. [L0671.011]
- For Campaign Alpha, targeting high-converting terms: set bid strategy to Maximize Revenue, apply high bids, set Shopping Campaign Priority to Low, and add negative keywords to block low-converting terms and universal negatives. [L0055.002]
- Alpha's Shopping campaign contains the full product set. [L0746.002]
- Alpha campaign setup, 2019 version: [L0243.033]
  1. Set campaign priority to Low. [L0243.033]
  2. Set daily budget to a higher amount (e.g., $30). [L0243.033]
  3. Set cost-per-click bids to a higher amount. [L0243.033]
  4. Populate the campaign with only high-converting, long-tail keywords (e.g., specific product model numbers, brand plus descriptor keywords). [L0243.033]
  5. Add weak and generic terms as negative keywords to prevent budget waste. [L0243.033]

#### Beta

- Beta campaigns target low-converting, generic or informational search terms, with low bidding to capture the remaining relevant traffic economically. Use negative keywords to block high-converting branded terms so they funnel to the alpha campaign instead. [L0225.003]
- Beta targets broader, lower-intent searches, for example general niche terms such as `surfboards`. [L0186.004]
- Beta holds the keywords that still convert but are weaker. [L0671.289]
- For Campaign Beta, targeting low-converting terms: apply low bids (lower than Campaign Alpha), set Shopping Campaign Priority to High, and add negative keywords to block high-converting terms from Campaign Alpha and universal negatives. [L0055.003]
- Beta setup, 2019 version: [L0243.034]
  1. Set campaign priority to High (Google checks this campaign first for matching searches). [L0243.034]
  2. Set daily budget to a lower amount (e.g., $17). [L0243.034]
  3. Set cost-per-click bids to lower amounts. [L0243.034]
  4. Include weak but still relevant keywords that might convert (e.g., broader product category keywords, variations). [L0243.034]
  5. Add strong and high-converting keywords as negative keywords so they are captured by the Alpha campaign instead. [L0243.034]

#### Worked Example (2019)

- *(Older advice, 2019)* For standup desks, `Hampton blue umbrella SKU 123` is a strong keyword (Alpha). The generic `umbrella` is blocked in Alpha as a negative keyword. In Beta, the generic term is allowed with a low bid. If someone searches `umbrella`, Beta captures it at low cost-per-click. If they search the exact `Hampton blue umbrella SKU 123`, it is blocked in Beta and goes to Alpha with the high bid. [L0243.036]

#### Alpha-Beta Procedure (2020)

*(Older advice, 2020)* [L0245.015]

1. In Google Ads, create an alpha campaign with your broad product feed. [L0245.015]
2. Create a separate beta campaign with high-priority, high-intent keywords. [L0245.015]
3. Set negative keywords at the ad group level (not the campaign level) to eliminate irrelevant searches from the alpha. [L0245.015]
4. Beta is checked first by Google before alpha routes traffic. [L0245.015]
5. This structure allows you to progressively refine the alpha as you identify underperforming keywords. [L0245.015]

#### Splitting Proven and Untested Products (2020)

- *(Older advice, 2020)* Use alpha campaigns for products that already sell and beta campaigns for testing. Exclude the proven products from beta so new products get their own budget. [L0468.114]
- Split Shopping campaigns into an alpha campaign for proven products and search terms that convert well, and a beta campaign for weaker or untested segments. Bid higher in the alpha campaign and lower in the beta campaign. [L0510.065]

### Negative Keywords and Routing

#### Routing Rules

- Do not manually move keywords between alpha and beta campaigns. Instead, adjust bid amounts upward in the beta campaign. Keyword routing happens automatically, based on your negative keyword setup and campaign priority settings. *(Older advice, 2024)* [L0276.059]
- Bidding control in Shopping works by adding negative keywords. High-converting terms are added as negatives to the Beta campaign so they are blocked there and fall through to Alpha, where bids are higher. [L0743.005]
- For a multi-brand store, the Beta campaign's negative list contains each brand name, each SKU number and each bestselling product name, so that those searches go to Alpha. Broad, unbranded searches such as a generic product description are then left for Beta. [L0746.030]
- Do not skip the Item ID subdivision step in either ad group. [L0746.028]

#### Negatives in Each Campaign

| Campaign | Negatives | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Alpha | Block low-converting terms and universal negatives | [L0055.002, L0225.002] |
| Alpha | Universal negatives only | [L0746.025] |
| Alpha | Weak and generic terms | [L0243.033] |
| Beta | High-intent terms: brand names you sell, product names you sell, SKU/MPN numbers | [L0186.005] |
| Beta | Brand names, SKU numbers, popular product names, strong product-name variants, and universal negatives | [L0746.025] |
| Beta | Branded terms as phrase match, for example `lifestyles`, plus universal negatives | [L0225.028] |
| Beta | Strong and high-converting keywords | [L0243.034] |

- Add all high-intent search terms (brand names you sell, product names you sell, SKU/MPN numbers) as negative keywords in Beta. [L0186.005]
- In the Alpha campaign, add only universal negatives: terms that should never match, for example course and videos for a merchandise store. [L0746.025]
- *(No year given)* Add universal negative keywords in both campaigns. [L0225.027, L0225.028]
- *(No year given)* Negative keyword for branded terms in beta, for example "lifestyles" as phrase match, to block them from beta and funnel to alpha. [L0225.028]
- *(No year given)* Negative keywords in the alpha campaign block weak or generic terms. [L0225.002]
- *(Older advice, 2019)* Negative keywords are added to the Alpha campaign to block weak and generic terms. [L0243.033]
- *(Older advice, 2020)* Negative keywords belong at the ad group level, not the campaign level. [L0245.015]
- Campaign-level negatives: Alpha and Beta negatives are set at campaign level in the build procedures. [L0746.025]

#### Negative Keyword Push (Sculpting)

1. Compare cost per click and conversion rate in the alpha and beta campaigns. Example figures: beta CPC $0.45 with a conversion rate of 0.64%, alpha CPC $1.93 with a conversion rate of 2.39%. ROAS (conversion value over cost) was 3.48 in alpha and 4.96 in beta. [L0745.023]
2. Open the beta campaign, go to Keywords, then Search terms, and show the terms that converted. [L0745.023]
3. Add every converting search term to the beta campaign as a negative exact keyword. [L0745.023]
4. Optionally move terms with strong click-through rate from beta to alpha as well. [L0745.023]
5. Result: converting terms are funneled into alpha, where bids are more aggressive for high-converting terms. [L0745.023]

### Campaign and Ad Group Naming

#### Naming Formats

| Format | Example | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Alpha, [Store Name] / Beta, [Store Name] | Standard campaign names | [L0186.006, L0186.007] |
| Campaign type, product category, target ROAS | `Alpha Shopping Infrared Sauna 3.3x` | [L0225.014] |
| Alpha Shopping [Category] [TargetROAS] | Alpha campaign template | [L0225.027] |
| Beta Shopping [Category] [LowerROAS] | Beta campaign template | [L0225.028] |
| Product name, campaign type, traffic source, country, target ROAS | `infrared saunas, shopping campaigns, cold traffic, USA, 3.6` | [L0327.021] |
| Priority and bid level | `Shopping - All Products - US - High Priority` | [L0742.034] |
| Course style | `alpha... Source A merch` | [L0743.020] |
| Course build | `alpha all products shopping`, `beta all products shopping` | [L0746.025] |

- Name each shopping campaign with three elements: campaign type (Alpha Shopping or Beta Shopping), product category (e.g., Infrared Sauna), and target ROAS (e.g., 3.3x). Example: `Alpha Shopping Infrared Sauna 3.3x`. This makes the campaign's purpose immediately clear when you review performance. [L0225.014]
- Include target ROAS in campaign names for quick reference and decision-making. Format: [Product name], [Campaign type], [Traffic source], [Country], [Target ROAS number]. This allows instant verification when reviewing performance. [L0327.021]
- *(Older advice, 2021-2022)* Give each funnel campaign a name that shows its priority and bid level, for example `Shopping - All Products - US - High Priority` for the lowest-bid campaign. Identical copies are otherwise hard to tell apart. The name has no effect on how ads are served. [L0742.034]
- Name each ad group after its campaign, for example `alpha` for the Alpha campaign and `beta` for the Beta campaign. Keep one ad group per Shopping campaign at the start. [L0743.030]
- Ad group names in the course build: `alpha all products` and `beta all products`. [L0746.025]
- Campaign naming for the Standard build: `Alpha, [Store Name]` and `Beta, [Store Name]`. [L0186.006, L0186.007]
- *(Older advice, 2021-2022)* When you copy a campaign, the copy's name gets a `#2` suffix. [L0742.043]

### Product Groups and Item ID Subdivision

#### The Waterfall Structure

- A new Google Shopping campaign starts with all products in one group at the same bid. This is a problem once the catalog holds many products, so the group should be split. [L0503.001]
- The waterfall keeps the structure in layers: all products, then brand, then item ID. Each lower layer can receive its own bid once enough data exists for that product, so bidding can be tuned down to the individual SKU. [L0503.012]

#### Waterfall Procedure

1. Open the shopping campaign, where all products sit in one group with the same bid. [L0503.004]
2. Click the plus sign to add a subdivision. [L0503.004, L0503.005]
3. Choose the split dimension: product category, brand, item ID or custom label. [L0503.004, L0503.005]
4. Split by brand first, selecting the brands you want, and then split further by item ID if needed. [L0503.004]
5. Set the same starting bid for every group. [L0503.004]
6. Open each brand group, add a subdivision, and drag in all of its item IDs, so every SKU becomes its own group. [L0503.004]
7. As data arrives for each product, adjust the bid per SKU. [L0503.004]

#### Split Options and Store Types

- In the Google Ads shopping campaign, the subdivision is added with the plus sign on the product group. The available split options are Product category, Brand, Item ID and Custom label. The Item ID option lists every individual product. [L0503.005]
- Custom labels can be left out when a shopping campaign is first launched, because they are rarely needed at that stage. Brand and item ID splits cover most early segmentation. [L0503.006]
- In a multi-brand store, select several brands in the brand split and then subdivide the selection by item ID. This narrows the groups down to individual products while keeping the brand structure. [L0503.007]
- For a store that sells only one brand, bids can be edited directly for each product group after the split. There is no need for a brand level. [L0503.008]
- Example: a multi-brand store started with 318 products in one group. After splitting by brand, each brand received its own bid, with $1 per brand used as the starting bid in the demo. [L0503.010]

#### Brand-to-SKU Procedure

1. Open a brand group. [L0503.011]
2. Add a subdivision. [L0503.011]
3. Drag in all item IDs for that brand. [L0503.011]
4. Repeat for every brand so each product ID can be bid separately. [L0503.011]

#### Item ID Subdivision (Alpha and Beta)

1. Inside the Alpha campaign, find the product group labelled All products. [L0186.010]
2. Click + (Add subdivision). [L0186.010]
3. Select Item ID. [L0186.010]
4. Select all items and save without editing any individual product bids at this stage. This gives you the future ability to adjust bids at the product level. [L0186.010]

- Enable the Item ID subdivision in the ad group. Click the plus icon next to All products, choose Add subdivision, set the dimension to Item ID, select all items, and click Save without editing bids so each product can receive its own CPC. Do this in the Alpha campaign as early as possible. [L0743.019]
- Subdivide by Item ID on the ad group page: click the plus next to Add subdivision, choose Item ID, tick the box to select all products, click Continue to edit bids, then Save. This gives per-product reporting and lets you adjust bids individually. [L0746.023]
- Do not skip the Item ID subdivision step in either ad group. It is easy to miss, but without it you cannot see or control results per product. [L0746.028]
- In a Google Shopping campaign, set product groups to individual products so that spend, clicks and sales can be tracked and bid per product. [L0671.014, L0671.288]
- Every product group should be checked for the catch-all "Everything else in" group. After each subdivision, make sure it contains no products (exclude it). Otherwise those products cannot receive individual bids and their performance cannot be seen. *(Older advice, 2021-2022)* [L0742.025]
- For products added to Shopify after alpha-beta setup: they appear in the everything-else or all-products section. Go to the Google Shopping setup lesson (module 6), create individual product campaigns for the newly added products, and they will no longer be grouped under everything-else. *(Older advice, 2025)* [L0255.047]
- Product group filter: in the ad group step, the product group can be filtered to show only selected products. As a starting point, leave it on All products in both campaigns, so every product is eligible in each. [L0743.031]
- Start with one ad group that includes all products in both the Alpha and Beta campaigns, with the ad group bid set to the campaign's starting CPC. [L0743.018]

### Launch with All Products

#### Single Campaign at Launch

- Keep all products in one Google Shopping campaign. A separate campaign for bestsellers only is usually not recommended. [L0359.071]
- Start with all products in the Shopping campaign so every product gets impressions. [L0551.040]
- Do not add manual keywords at the start of a Shopping campaign. Google reads the catalog and decides which searches to show products for. *(Older advice, 2020)* [L0551.039]
- *(Older advice, 2018)* A new store with about 200 products from approved suppliers should begin with one single Google Shopping campaign. Its goal is data on impressions, clicks, sales, and clicks without sales. Segmentation by brand or category should wait until that data is available. [L0466.024]
- *(Older advice, 2018)* Procedure for the single launch campaign: [L0466.025]
  1. Launch a single Google Shopping campaign that includes all products. [L0466.025]
  2. Review the dashboards for impressions, clicks, sales, search terms, and which products get clicks but no sales. [L0466.025]
  3. Remove negative keywords that bring irrelevant traffic. [L0466.025]
  4. Split the campaign into two campaigns, Alpha and Beta, using the data. [L0466.025]
  5. Analyze the data every two weeks, and segment further by brand, category, bestsellers or price tier as the data supports. [L0466.025]
- *(Older advice, 2020)* Procedure for initial Shopping data: [L0551.040]
  1. Start with all products in the Shopping campaign so every product gets impressions. [L0551.040]
  2. Review the search terms that trigger clicks and sales after the ads start running. [L0551.040]
  3. Add irrelevant search terms as negative keywords. [L0551.040]
  4. Increase budget on the products and keywords that produce clicks and sales. [L0551.040]
  5. Check the numbers in Google Ads so that growth stays profitable. [L0551.040]

#### Large Catalog Launch

- *(Older advice, 2021)* Upload the full available product catalog before increasing ad spend. A larger catalog gives Google more products to test and optimize. [L0247.049]
- *(Older advice, 2021)* Launch procedure for a new store with 500+ products: [L0270.056]
  1. Create an alpha campaign with all products. [L0270.056]
  2. Create a beta campaign with all products. [L0270.056]
  3. Create a shopping campaign with all products. [L0270.056]
  4. Let all campaigns run with $10-30 per day budget. [L0270.056]
  5. Use performance data over 2 weeks to identify which specific products perform well. [L0270.056]
  6. Optimize by lowering cost-per-click on underperformers and raising it on strong products. [L0270.056]
  7. Never exclude products initially; let data guide allocation. [L0270.056]
- *(Older advice, 2024)* Launch a large catalog this way: [L0471.010]
  1. Create one ad group named `All Products` that contains every product. [L0471.010]
  2. Track performance by product. [L0471.010]
  3. Raise bids on products with a strong return on ad spend and lower bids on weak ones. [L0471.010]
- *(Older advice, 2023)* Start with a narrow feed of about the top 20 products instead of a large catalog of around 1,000, with a daily budget of 20 USD for each alpha and beta campaign. Choose the products by potential profit or by the best-selling products on future competitor stores. [L0470.027]
- *(Older advice, 2023)* Creating hundreds of ad groups with one product each, to get very granular analytics, limits what Google's algorithm can learn, unless the budget is very large. Single-keyword ad groups per product are outdated and should not be used for small budgets. [L0470.095]

#### Structure by Catalog Type

- The alpha-beta structure with all products is the standard launch for a store that sells several brands. The two campaigns both contain the full product set. Products are not split between them. Only the search terms each campaign catches differ, and negative keywords enforce that split. [L0746.002]
- A store that sells only its own brand does not really need the Alpha and Beta split, because all searches are for the same brand. The structure is still worth learning, and the same negative keyword logic applies to any store that sells several brands. [L0746.029]
- Alpha and beta product structuring is an advanced Google Shopping setup. Learn it after basic Shopping campaigns are running. [L0359.070]
- A typical setup with a split by sub-niche: *(Older advice, 2022)* structure Google Shopping campaigns as Alpha (testing) and Beta (optimized). Start with one of each, then break them up by sub-niche, product type or supplier, based on incoming data and not assumptions. [L0249.054]
- A typical e-commerce Google Shopping funnel runs from the Shopify product feed into Google Merchant Center, then into Alpha and Beta shopping campaigns, then to product pages. A two- or three-campaign structure separates branded, generic and specific SKU-level keywords. [L0454.014]

### Approval, Activation and Timing

#### Before Launch

- Create Google Shopping campaigns only after all products are fully approved in Google Merchant Center. If product approval is pending or Google has requested changes, fix those issues and get full approval before proceeding. [L0186.002]
- Before enabling the campaigns, most products should be approved in Google Merchant Center. Not every product needs to be approved. Products that are not approved simply do not show. [L0742.044] *(Older advice, 2021-2022)*
- The Google Ads account and the Merchant Center account are already linked, so the product feed loads automatically. If several feeds exist, for example one per country, select the correct one. The country of sale defaults to the country of the Google Ads account. [L0742.038] *(Older advice, 2021-2022)*
- The Merchant Center holds the product feed that Shopping campaigns use. It must be linked to the Google Ads account, and the correct Merchant Center account must be selected when creating each Shopping campaign. [L0746.021]
- Only one funnel should run at a time. Pause older or duplicate Shopping campaigns before running the new structure. Two funnels competing in the same account confuse Google. *(Older advice, 2021-2022)* [L0744.021]

#### Pausing and Enabling

1. Pause all funnel campaigns while settings, bids and negative keyword lists are being applied. This keeps ads from running with incomplete settings. [L0742.042] *(Older advice, 2021-2022)*
2. Once products are approved in Google Merchant Center, enable the paused campaigns. Ads begin delivering over the next few hours. [L0742.031] *(Older advice, 2021-2022)*
3. Enable the campaigns only once the funnel is fully configured. [L0742.042] *(Older advice, 2021-2022)*

#### Copying a Campaign

*(Older advice, 2021-2022)* [L0742.043]

1. Use Edit, then Copy, then Paste to duplicate a campaign. The copy keeps its ad groups, product groups, bids, priority and negative keyword assignments. [L0742.043]
2. The copy's name gets a `#2` suffix. [L0742.043]
3. The paste dialog can pause the new campaigns. [L0742.043]
4. Copying a large campaign can take several minutes, so wait for the progress bar to finish. [L0742.043]

#### Approval Timing

- Campaigns may show ads under review. Approval typically takes around 30 minutes but can take up to a few days. Once approved, impressions and clicks should start, followed by purchases as optimization continues. [L0186.011]
- Wait about one day for approval, then open Ads and extensions to check the approval status. Impressions and clicks can take a few days to start arriving. [L0746.025]
- Wait for the campaigns to be approved before continuing. [L0743.020]
- Ads begin delivering within a few hours of enabling. *(Older advice, 2021-2022)* [L0742.044]

### Optimization and Judging Performance

- Judge Alpha and Beta together by conversion rate and ROAS, not ROAS alone. Beta can show a higher ROAS from very cheap clicks while converting far less often. Example: beta at $0.45 CPC and a 0.64% conversion rate versus alpha at $1.93 CPC and a 2.39% conversion rate, with ROAS of 4.96 in beta and 3.48 in alpha. Converting search terms should be moved into alpha. [L0745.035]
- Alpha and beta are reviewed and optimized together during the weekly audit. [L0715.023]
- Compare cost per click and conversion rate in the alpha and beta campaigns, then run the negative keyword push above. [L0745.023]
- Analyze the data every two weeks, and segment further by brand, category, bestsellers or price tier as the data supports. *(Older advice, 2018)* [L0466.025]
- Do not manually move keywords between campaigns. Adjust bid amounts upward in the beta campaign instead. *(Older advice, 2024)* [L0276.059]
- Impressions, clicks and sales should be read per product once the Item ID subdivision is in place. [L0746.023, L0671.014]

### The Google Shopping Funnel: Overview

#### What the Funnel Is

- For high-ticket products, the only Google Shopping structure described as consistently effective is search query level bidding, also called the shopping funnel. Other Shopping approaches are generally built for lower-ticket products. *(Older advice, 2021-2022)* [L0740.001]
- Search query level bidding also goes by the names alpha beta and inverted funnel. These are informal labels for the same strategy. Use the official name when searching for or comparing sources. *(Older advice, 2021-2022)* [L0740.004]
- Standard Google Shopping ads promote one product at a time, so broad top-of-funnel searches are rarely ready to consider a single product. Standard Shopping ads suit middle- and bottom-of-funnel searches only. *(Older advice, 2021-2022)* [L0740.005]
- The alpha-beta campaign structure is the answer to Shopping's main limitation. You cannot pick keywords or set keyword-level bids. By splitting campaigns and using negatives to funnel, you effectively create high-bid and low-bid keyword groups, even though Google picks which searches trigger your ads. [L0225.031]
- Use two Shopping campaigns. An Alpha campaign for high-converting terms (brand names, product names, SKU numbers) and a Beta campaign for broad, generic, lower-converting terms, so that bids can be set differently for each group of keywords. [L0743.004, L0186.003]
- Use two Shopping campaigns that both contain the full product set: an Alpha campaign for the highest-converting searches (brand names, product names, SKU numbers) and a Beta campaign for broader, lower-converting searches. Products are not split between them. Only the search terms each campaign catches differ, and negative keywords enforce that split. [L0746.002]
- Create two campaigns (Alpha and Beta). Google Shopping ads use product feed data, titles, descriptions and site content, not positive keywords. Google decides what searches show your ads. The two-campaign structure lets you control bidding indirectly with negative keywords. High-intent searches go into Alpha (higher bids) and broad searches into Beta (lower bids). [L0186.003]
- Shopping campaigns are split into two parts to separate high and low bids. This is the core of the funnel. [L0225.001]

#### The Funnel in Sequence

1. Google reads the product feed submitted through Merchant Center. [L0746.001, L0714.008]
2. Beta (High priority) is checked first and blocks searches that match its negatives. [L0746.006, L0746.008]
3. Searches blocked by Beta fall through to Alpha (Low priority), where the higher bid applies. [L0243.035, L0746.006]
4. Searches that match neither negative stay in Beta at the lower bid. [L0243.036]
5. Converting search terms are moved into Alpha by negative exact keywords. [L0745.023]
6. Each campaign is judged on conversion rate and ROAS together. [L0745.035]

#### Alpha-Beta Example

- Alpha example: high-intent searches (brand names, product names, SKU/MPN numbers) produce ROAS around 15x, so start with a CPC bid of $0.40. Beta example: broader, lower-intent searches (general niche terms such as `surfboards`) produce ROAS around 8x, so start with a CPC bid of $0.20, about half of Alpha. [L0186.004]
- Beta negatives push high-intent terms to Alpha. Example: a store that sells several brands lists each brand name, SKU number and bestselling product name as Beta negatives. [L0746.030, L0186.005]

### How Shopping Ads Work

- Shopping campaigns offer no direct keyword targeting, so you cannot give Google a list of search terms your ads should show for. Your only direct control over which searches trigger your ads is excluding terms with negative keywords. [L1074.001]
- Google matches Shopping ads to searches by reading the product data you supply. This is usually accurate but not always. Google does not judge search intent or value the way a merchant does, so the merchant has to steer it with negative keywords. [L1074.003]
- Google picks the search terms to show for from the product titles and descriptions in the submitted feed, so those fields matter most. [L1165.013]
- Feed quality, especially titles and attributes, controls which searches your products appear for. [L1328.003]
- The keywords used for matching come from the product pages in Merchant Center. The only keywords to add are negative keywords for searches you do not want. [L1097.032]
- Shopping does not use keywords the way search ads do, so relevance depends on product titles, data and category. [L1114.054]
- To change which search terms trigger a product, edit its product page content so it includes those keywords, then let the feed update. [L1277.073]
- Shopping listings are ranked by search term and product data. A niche with few brand searches is not a problem by itself. Focus on the generic product keyword and keep the same alpha/beta structure. [L1090.105]
- Product listing ads mostly target long-tail keywords. Ranking in Shopping is a different challenge from organic search and is generally easier. *Older advice (2018).* [L1274.065]
- Shopping ads need no copywriting. Once the store is connected to Google Ads, the ads are generated automatically from the product name, price and store name. *Older advice (2019).* [L1069.079]
- Alpha and beta Shopping campaigns need no manually entered keywords, because keywords are pulled from the product feed. Brand and search text campaigns are the only places where keywords are entered by hand. *Older advice (2023).* [L0855.010]
- Within Google Ads, Shopping is typically the largest and most frequently used campaign type for dropshipping stores, so it deserves the most attention when optimizing. *Older advice (2021-22).* [L1494.002]

### Choosing the Campaign Type

| Option | Status and use | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Standard Shopping | Core structure for product campaigns. Per-product reporting is possible. | [L0854.052, L1092.059] |
| Smart Shopping | Phased out by Google. Do not use. | [L0854.052] |
| Smart campaigns (goal-based) | Suit beginners who will not spend time optimizing and want to launch in a few minutes. Trade advertiser control for visibility and fast launch. | [L1336.003] |
| Custom campaigns | For advanced advertisers who want full customization and maximum profitability. Every setting stays under the advertiser's control. | [L1336.004] |
| Performance Max | Does not show product-level data. | [L1092.059] |

- Google Ads shows predefined smart goals every time a new campaign is created, not only during the first account setup. Advertisers must go through this selection step each time. [L1336.001]
- The campaign goal screen offers Sales, Leads and Website traffic as smart goal options. A fourth option, create a campaign without a goal, is at the bottom of the screen. [L1336.002]
- Google Shopping ad types for product campaigns are Normal, Dynamic Ads, and YouTube Shopping and Gmail Shopping. Choose by goal: standard product ads, retargeting, or placements on video and email. [L1033.008]
- Per-product bid control is not the default in Google Ads. It requires building the Shopping campaigns in the specific structure described in the Google Shopping setup lesson, so existing campaigns may need to be rebuilt. *Older advice (2023).* [L0855.013]
- Interface changes in Google Ads do not change the campaign structure or the bid strategies. *Older advice (2025).* [L1116.025]

### Campaign Creation and Settings

- When Google Ads or Shopping shows Continue instead of Enabled during setup, click Continue and check the status again. Ads that are already running may show Enabled afterward. *Older advice (2023).* [L1094.047]
- Search partners are non-Google websites that belong to the search network and display Google ads. To keep Shopping ads running only on google.com, exclude search partners along with YouTube, Gmail and Discover. [L0746.035]
- The language setting in a Google Ads campaign controls which user language preferences see the ads, not the language of the website. For a non-English market, select that language and write the ad text and keywords in it. *Older advice (2021-22).* [L1342.045]
- Google Shopping ads must be either already live or still pending approval before the launch date. Once approved, they start generating impressions and sales. [L1393.003]

### Choosing the Structure: Alpha and Beta

- The two-tier principle: the Alpha campaign targets strong search terms with higher bids. The Beta campaign picks up weaker, more general terms with low bids, accepting a lower CTR and lower conversion rate on it. [L0805.015]
- Shopping campaigns are split into Alpha and Beta campaigns, each with its own Return on Ad Spend (ROAS) target. Alpha is the core product-level campaign and Beta is the testing campaign. [L0867.002]
- Split the Shopping setup into separate alpha and beta campaigns, each with its own bid and budget, so you can compare them. [L0808.058]
- A high-priority Alpha campaign captures brand, product name and SKU searches. A Beta campaign captures general terms. Negative keywords in Beta keep specific searches out of it. [L0966.079]
- Alpha and beta both receive impressions and clicks. They split keywords by quality, and each campaign has its own report. *Older advice (2019).* [L1002.039]
- Alpha and beta keep the same structure even when alpha has few keywords. Use a shared budget rather than changing the structure. *Older advice (2021).* [L1090.104]
- Use the Alpha Beta campaign structure for Google Shopping. *Older advice (2025).* [L1116.025]
- Use an alpha and beta structure in Google Ads. Keep alpha for targeted searches and beta for broader searches, and add negative keywords to both. *Older advice (2020).* [L0961.057]
- A simplified single Google Ads campaign that lets Google decide where to spend the budget is not the best approach. Turn it off and rebuild the account using the alpha and beta structure. *Older advice (2020).* [L0961.056]
- A standard Shopping setup in Google Ads uses three campaign types: Generic, Brand and SKU. Alpha and Beta Shopping campaigns should follow this structure as the default. [L1033.002]
- A basic starting setup has four campaigns: Google Shopping alpha, Google Shopping beta, Google remarketing and Meta remarketing. Avoid testing many other formats, such as cold display or cold Meta ads, at the start. *Older advice (2025).* [L0972.063]

#### Launch Structure

- At launch, put all products into both the Alpha and Beta Shopping campaigns. Alpha and Beta form a two-tier structure. A three-tier structure also works, but two tiers is the default setup. [L0971.093]
- Start Shopping with two campaigns, alpha and beta, that both include all products. Do not split Shopping campaigns by product category at the start. *Older advice (2025).* [L0972.061]
- Start with one alpha and one beta campaign covering all products in one feed. Optimize them over time rather than splitting products one per campaign. *Older advice (2022).* [L0969.066]

### Shared Budgets and Priority

| Setting | Alpha | Beta |
|---|---|---|
| Role | Strong terms, brand, product name, SKU | General terms, testing |
| Priority | High | Lower |
| Bid | Higher | Low |
| Negative keywords | Blocks lower-converting terms | Receives blocked terms; specific searches excluded |
| Source | [L0966.079, L0805.015, L0808.058] | [L0966.079, L0805.015, L0808.058] |

- Alpha and beta should share one budget, so one campaign cannot consume the whole budget. Set campaign priority correctly during setup, since mismatched priorities let one campaign eat the budget. *Older advice (2023).* [L0804.075]
- Keep alpha and beta from competing and driving up cost per click by using negative keywords and campaign priority levels. Without them, the campaigns bid against each other. *Older advice (2022).* [L0854.045]
- No fixed minimum budget is required to start a Shopping campaign, but a larger budget produces data faster. Each new campaign must be tested under its own conditions and product set, even for advertisers who already run other accounts. [L1341.004]
- A small share of search terms, around 5%, appearing in the alpha campaign when they should be in beta under a shared budget is not a reason to restructure. A leak that small is not enough data to pin down a cause, and budget differences would usually produce a much larger share. Keep the structure, keep adding negative keywords, and reassess later. *Older advice (2021).* [L1090.145]

### Negative Keywords

- Use negative keywords in both alpha and beta campaigns to block searches that belong elsewhere. *Older advice (2020).* [L0961.057]
- Blocking many cheaper or lower-value searches with negative keywords can hurt more than help, because it may block searches that would have converted. [L0805.015]
- Add negative keywords and ad group bid adjustments after the store has data, not at the start. *Older advice (2020).* [L1111.113]
- Negative keywords are the only keywords to add to Shopping campaigns, and only for searches you do not want. [L1097.032]

### Bids and Starting CPC

- Example starting bids are $1.00 for alpha and $0.50 for beta, with a starting point of about $0.50 to $1.00 CPC. [L0808.058]
- The launch phase is about buying data, not expecting profit. Keyword and product research cannot predict the actual cost per click or the real conversion rate, so the account has to be launched and tested to learn these values. [L1341.001]
- High bids that produce no clicks signal that competitors are bidding more aggressively. Market data reveals both bid competitiveness and conversion rate competitiveness, so the campaign must be tested to find out. [L1341.003]
- For standard Shopping, keep ad rotation set to optimize for best performing ads. *Older advice (2024).* [L1115.039]
- Lower the cost per click for a product group when it takes too much of the budget. *Older advice (2020).* [L0852.061]
- Set bids per product. For example, raise a cost per click from 0.20 USD to 0.25 USD on a product that needs more impressions. *Older advice (2020).* [L1277.072]
- To change bids per product, split the catalog into product groups so each product or brand can get its own cost per click. Raise the bid only on products that get impressions but too few clicks or that have low visibility. *Older advice (2021).* [L1112.008]
- A product with no impressions should be checked for search demand, relevance and competition before its bid is raised. [L1114.054]

### Product Groups and Item ID Subdivision

#### Subdivision Options

- When adding a subdivision to a Shopping ad group, the options are product type, category, brand and Item ID. Choose Item ID to break the ad group down by individual product, so each product gets its own reporting row and its own bid. [L0746.036]
- In Google Shopping campaigns, each product group corresponds to one product. *Older advice (2020).* [L0852.061]
- In standard Shopping campaigns, place each product in its own product group so impressions, clicks and sales are visible per product. Performance Max does not show product-level data. *Older advice (2022).* [L1092.059]
- Split product groups by individual product so spend and return are visible per product in Google Ads. *Older advice (2020).* [L1277.072]

#### The Everything Else Node

- When a Shopping product group is subdivided, Google Ads adds an Everything else node. It is set to Excluded and carries no bid. Products that match none of the named subdivisions fall into this node and do not serve, so every product should be placed in a labelled group. *Older advice (2021-22).* [L0747.025]
- Check the product count in the Everything Else in All Products group. If all products are split out at product level, that group should be empty. *Older advice (2024).* [L0836.028]
- Check whether an All products product group sits alongside individually listed products in the same ad group. If it does, pause the All products group so products are not counted twice. *Older advice (2020).* [L0852.064]

### Launch

- Launch campaigns with the full product catalog in one alpha and one beta campaign. Then remove products based on data as clicks and conversions come in. Do not pre-select products before there is data. [L0941.069]
- Start Google Shopping campaigns with the full product catalog as soon as the products are uploaded and the feed is set up. Driving traffic to the homepage with broad keywords is expensive and brings the least qualified buyers. *Older advice (2020).* [L1277.071]
- Keep ad structure simple at the start, with all products in the Alpha and Beta campaigns. Negative keywords and ad group bid adjustments can be added after the store has data. *Older advice (2020).* [L1111.113]
- Launch three core campaigns on Google Ads first, before any social traffic: product listing ads (PLAs), search text ads on profitable terms, and search audience campaigns with retargeting. Once they work on Google, copy them over to Bing Ads. *Older advice (2019 onward, undated source).* [L1203.008]

### Google Shopping Funnel and Process Overview

1. Connect the store to Google Ads. Shopping ads are then generated automatically from product name, price and store name, with no copywriting needed. [L1069.079]
2. Submit the feed. Google reads product titles, descriptions and attributes to decide which searches your products match, and it uses the Merchant Center product pages for matching keywords. [L1165.013, L1097.032]
3. Launch the full catalog in one alpha and one beta campaign, with the shared budget and priority set correctly. [L0941.069, L0804.075]
4. Build the PLA alpha/beta pattern. Run two campaigns per product listing ad setup. The alpha campaign uses negative keywords to block lower-converting search terms, and the beta campaign receives those terms. Every PLA campaign is typically duplicated this way. [L1203.010]
5. Compare channels. In the owner's Google campaigns, Shopping converted much better than Search, with a strong conversion rate. For a store running both, Google Shopping is the channel to scale first. [L1077.049]
6. Optimize with data. Remove products that do not perform, split product groups by Item ID, adjust bids on products that need impressions, and add negative keywords for unwanted searches. [L0941.069, L0746.036, L1112.008, L1097.032]
7. Copy proven campaigns to Bing Ads after they work on Google. [L1203.008]

Each PLA setup also follows the long-tail principle: product listing ads mostly target long-tail keywords, and the alpha and beta structure applies. [L1274.065, L1203.010]

### Where Sources Disagree

- **Full catalog at launch versus product-level split from the start.** Launch with the full catalog in alpha and beta, then split products by individual product once data arrives [L0941.069, L1277.071, L1111.113]. Older 2020 advice also gives a per-product bid split from the outset [L1277.072, L0852.061]. Apply the full-catalog launch first. Apply the per-product split when there is data to justify each product's bid.
- **Brand split versus product split.** Source B's older default splits Shopping campaigns by brand within three priority levels (high, medium and low). Split by price, margin or product type only when there is a specific reason for that product group [L0879.024]. Source A's guidance splits standard Shopping by individual product so that performance is visible per product [L1092.059, L0746.036]. A brand split is also named as a valid option for bid control [L1112.008]. Use the brand split where the three-priority-level structure is in use. Use the per-product split for standard Shopping.
- **Number of campaign tiers.** The default is two tiers, alpha and beta. A three-tier structure also works [L0971.093]. The standard Shopping setup named as Generic, Brand and SKU [L1033.002] and the three priority levels named by Source B [L0879.024] are both options. The basic starting setup of four campaigns adds remarketing campaigns on Google and Meta [L0972.063]. Start with two tiers. Add the others as the account needs them.
- **Negative keywords.** Negative keywords are added to both campaigns from the start [L0961.057]. Adding many negative keywords can block searches that would have converted, so they should be used with care [L0805.015]. Negative keywords and bid adjustments can wait until there is data [L1111.113].
- **Smart Shopping versus smart campaigns.** Smart Shopping as a campaign type is phased out and should not be used [L0854.052]. Smart campaigns offered on the goal screen are described as suitable for beginners [L1336.003]. Advanced advertisers should use custom campaigns [L1336.004].
- **Starting bid examples.** The 2026 example uses $1.00 for alpha and $0.50 for beta, with a starting range of $0.50 to $1.00 CPC [L0808.058]. The 2020 example raises one product's cost per click from 0.20 USD to 0.25 USD [L1277.072]. These are examples for different situations. Neither is a fixed rule.

## Search-Intent Shopping Funnel (Low/Medium/High Value Campaigns)

### Search intent and value tiers

- **Older (2021-22):** Search intent is the purchase intent behind a search term. It must be judged for every term from keyword research, whether for paid ads or SEO, and it decides how much a click from that term is worth to the business. [L0739.018]
- **Older (2021-22):** The same product can match searches with very different purchase intent. A broad category search shows little buying intent, a search with size and feature descriptors shows more, and a search with brand and model name shows the strongest buying intent for the exact product. [L0741.010]
- **Older (2021-22):** Search intent differs between high-ticket and low-ticket products, so the customer journey and the bidding approach must differ too. A method that works for cheap products can overspend badly on expensive ones. [L0740.003]
- **Older (2021-22):** Google does not sort search terms into value levels by buying intent and cares about this less than the advertiser does. The advertiser must therefore tell Google when to show ads and when not to. [L1074.004]
- **Older (2021-22):** Google Shopping suits middle- and bottom-of-funnel search terms. Branded and product-specific queries bring largely relevant traffic, while generic top-of-funnel terms, such as a broad category phrase sent to one product page, usually do not convert. Exclude such terms from Shopping and address them through another channel such as content. [L1456.006]
- Tag each search term by buying journey stage: research (top of funnel), comparing (middle of funnel) or ready to buy (bottom of funnel). Top-of-funnel terms can be valuable for awareness, but they usually convert less and should be judged against that. [L0876.024]

#### Value tier table

**Older (2021-22):** Three value tiers classify every search term.

| Value tier | Intent | Typical length | What the term identifies | Example (own) | Bid priority |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Low | Ambiguous; the searcher may want images, repairs, used items, rentals or information | 1 to 2 words | Only a product type | coffee grinder | Lowest |
| Medium | Specific; the searcher has narrowed the choice | 3 to 5 words, sometimes more | A group of products defined by type plus attributes such as size, capacity, zones or features | burr coffee grinder with 300 g hopper | Middle |
| High | Clear; the searcher wants one product | Brand plus model name, part number, SKU or another unique identifier | A single product | Acme Pro 500 burr grinder | Highest |

[L0739.019]

#### Low value terms

- **Older (2021-22):** Low value terms usually have a generic one- or two-word wording, so the searcher may only be browsing or may need service for a product bought elsewhere. Clicks on them cost the bid but rarely lead to a sale, so the chance of conversion is unknown. [L0739.020]
- **Older (2021-22):** Low value terms have ambiguous intent and are usually one or two words, so it is unclear what the searcher wants. They can still convert, but at a lower rate. [L0740.009]
- **Older (2021-22):** Shoppers sometimes click a store's ad for a product they bought from someone else, expecting help with service or a wider range, so a click does not mean a buyer. Some clicks from broad terms will bring contacts you cannot serve, which raises the real cost per sale. Include these unrelated contacts when judging whether a search term is profitable. [L0741.019]

#### Medium value terms

- **Older (2021-22):** Medium value terms add attributes such as size, capacity, zone count or feature, which shows real buying intent and points to a group of matching products. The retailer can reasonably expect that a visitor from such a term will buy something similar from its range. [L0739.021]
- **Older (2021-22):** Medium value terms show clearer intent, such as a product type combined with a size or feature. They still fit several products in the catalogue, so their conversion chance is higher than for low value terms but lower than for high value terms. [L0740.010]

#### High value terms

- **Older (2021-22):** High value terms name one product, either by brand plus model name or by part number, SKU or another unique identifier. If a brand sells several near-identical products, a brand-plus-description term is worth less than one containing the exact model identifier. [L0739.022]
- **Older (2021-22):** High value terms match exactly one product in the catalogue, typically a brand name combined with a specific model name. Because the intent is certain, they have the highest conversion chance and the highest value to the business. [L0740.011]
- **Older (2021-22):** A high-value search term is one that matches a single product, typically brand plus model number, part number, SKU or another unique identifier. If a brand has several products matching a brand-plus-description search, that term is worth somewhat less than one containing the unique identifier. [L0741.012]
- **Older (2021-22):** A search that combines a brand name with a product description is high value only if that brand sells just one product matching the description. If the brand has several near-identical models, treat that term as slightly lower value than a term containing the exact model number, part number or SKU. [L0739.031]
- **Older (2021-22):** A brand name plus a descriptive term without the model number counts as high value only if that brand has a single product matching the description. If the brand has several matching products, treat the term as somewhat lower value and check the brand's range before assigning value. [L0741.023]

#### Classifying a search term

- **Older (2021-22):** To classify a Shopping search term, count how many products in the catalogue it would fit. A term that matches only one product is high value, a product type narrowed by size or feature is medium value, and a broad generic word that could serve many unrelated purposes is low value. [L0740.021]
- **Older (2021-22):** Classify each search term by how many products it could match: many products means low value, one product group defined by attributes means medium value, and one exact product means high value. Examples from the same source: *walking shoes* is low, *waterproof trail walking shoes women size 10* is medium, and *Trailmax X3 women trail shoe size 10* is high. [L0739.023]
- **Older (2021-22):** Search terms are valued by how precisely they identify what the buyer wants. Low value terms are ambiguous and typically one or two words. Medium value terms identify a group of products and usually have three to five or more words. High value terms match exactly one product through brand plus model name, part number or SKU. Use this three-tier classification to decide how much each search term is worth to bid on. [L0741.011]
- **Older (2021-22):** Example ladder for a surfboard store: *surfboard* is a low-value term because the intent is unclear. *6 foot performance short board* is a medium-value term that narrows the product type and size. A brand plus model name such as *Channel Islands OG Flyer surfboard* is a high-value term that points to one specific product. [L0740.020]
- **Older (2021-22):** Example with one product, an inflatable paddleboard. A one-word term like *paddleboard* is low value. A term with size and type like *inflatable paddleboard 12 ft solo* is medium value. A term with brand plus model number is high value. Each step narrows the match to fewer products and shows stronger buying intent. [L0741.017]
- **Older (2021-22), procedure:**
  1. Export the search terms from your keyword research.
  2. For each term, decide whether it names only a product type, a product group defined by attributes, or one specific product through brand plus model or part number.
  3. Label each term low, medium or high value.
  4. Set the highest bids for high value terms, moderate bids for medium value terms, and limit bids on low value terms.
  5. Add negative keywords for terms with no buying intent for your products, and review the terms that trigger your ads.

  [L0739.029]

#### Share of traffic

- **Older (2021-22):** In any single market, only about 10% of search traffic is high value at a given time. Medium value traffic is slightly larger than high value traffic, and about 75% of traffic is low value. Expect most search traffic to be low value and budget accordingly. [L0739.024, L0741.015]
- **Older (2021-22):** At any given time, the bottom of the funnel usually represents only about 10% of most markets, while the majority of potential buyers sit at the top of the funnel. [L0740.007]
- **Older (2021-22):** For high-ticket dropshipping, keywords are usually sorted into three value levels: low, medium and high. Three or four levels are most common. More are possible but rarely needed. [L0740.008]
- **Older (2021-22):** Competitors and the market are not the only variable: the same tiers apply to any product, and a term's value comes from what it identifies, not from its brand alone. [L0742.003]

  *Note: L0742.003 states that the funnel segments search intent, not brand ownership; branding is one way to see the difference in specificity, and unbranded product lines can use the same three-level split.*

### Bidding by value

- **Older (2021-22):** Bid more for search terms with a higher chance of converting. Low value terms need many more clicks per sale, which raises the cost per sale. Bidding the same amount on every tier means spending far more for fewer conversions and wastes budget on low value terms. [L0739.027, L0741.013]
- **Older (2021-22):** In the shopping funnel, bid the most on high value terms, a middle amount on medium value terms, and the least on low value terms. Low value terms are not dropped, but they are bid cheaply because they convert at a lower rate. [L0740.012]
- **Older (2021-22):** Bids are set by value to the business. High value terms get high bids to win the auction. Low value terms get low bids to limit cost, because they have a low chance of conversion. [L0742.022]
- **Older (2021-22):** On high value search terms, bid high enough to win the first position in the Shopping results, but only when the store is well optimized for conversions and outperforms competitors. Without that, the high bid will not turn into profitable sales. [L0740.014]
- **Older (2021-22):** When one bid applies to all relevant search terms, raising the bid to win high value traffic also raises the cost of low value traffic. This coupling is why each keyword value level needs its own bid. [L0740.022]
- **Older (2021-22):** A standard Shopping ad structure charges the same bid for every keyword level, so the same cost per click is paid for low value and high value searches. This overpays on low value traffic and erodes profitability. [L0740.006]
- **Older (2021-22), mistake:** Targeting large amounts of low value traffic makes Shopping campaigns unprofitable, because spend grows faster than sales. Aim to capture as much high value traffic as possible, an acceptable share of medium value traffic, and limit exposure to low value traffic. [L0739.026]
- **Older (2021-22):** Competitors running a basic Shopping setup pay similar amounts for every keyword and must spend heavily on high value terms to stay competitive, which leaves them less profit per sale. A store that bids by keyword value and keeps more margin per sale can therefore outbid them for longer. [L0740.023]
- **Older (2021-22):** Most competitors pay the same average bid for branded and generic queries, so they lose money on the generic ones. Segmenting and bidding low on generic terms lets you keep those clicks at a positive ROI while they do not. [L1328.011]
- Searches that trigger the same Shopping campaign do not convert equally. Specific branded queries can convert around 5-10%, while generic queries may convert near 0.5%. Because of this spread, each search group needs a different bid. [L1328.004]
- Example: the specific branded term *Oakley Holbrook men's sunglasses* with high intent. A 0.50 USD bid won only about 300 clicks because competitors outbid it. Winning every click for this term could lift revenue from about 1,000 USD to about 3,000 USD for the same effort. [L1328.006]
- Bid high on specific, high-intent branded terms so you capture every impression, as long as the product stays inside your profitable ROI range. Bid low on generic, low-intent terms so they bring traffic without large losses. [L1328.007]
- Bid less on generic queries, such as a search for a generic product type, and more on branded queries, because branded searchers show stronger purchase intent. Example in the same pattern: bid less on a generic query for a standard kitchen knife set and more on the brand name of the same seller. The same logic applies to every account structure. [L0454.015]
- Searches for an exact product name, model number or SKU convert much better than searches for a general category term. Budget should therefore move toward brand names, product names and SKU numbers, and generic or irrelevant terms should be excluded. [L0626.008]
- Broad generic searches convert poorly because the shopper may not want the specific item shown. Searches for product names, brand names or SKU numbers convert much better and should receive the budget. [L0857.002]
- Broad keywords usually have a low click-through rate because the ad does not match what was searched. Google Shopping shows the exact product, so specific product or niche keyword matches tend to have a higher CTR. [L0857.003]
- Decide which keywords to expand based on whether their clicks turn into sales, not on click count alone. If clicks do not convert, add the terms as negatives or lower their CPC. [L0837.050]
- Brand, product-name and SKU searches convert well because the shopper already knows what they want. These searches are the main source of sales for lesser-known brands. [L0966.080]
- **Older (2019):** High-intent keywords such as brand names, product names and SKUs get fewer searches but convert better, so it is acceptable to spend more on them. Generic terms should receive the smaller share of the budget. [L1002.040]

### Campaign priority and bid inversion

- Campaign priority tells Google the order in which to evaluate identical campaigns during auction entry. Google checks the High priority campaign first, then Medium, then Low, and enters the first campaign where the search term is not blocked by negative keywords. **Older (2021-22):** [L0742.005]
- **Older (2021-22), mistake:** Campaign priority settings are inverted relative to search value. The low-value campaign gets High priority, the medium-value campaign gets Medium priority, and the high-value campaign gets Low priority. Getting this wrong breaks the whole funnel. [L0742.004]
- **Older (2021-22):** Without a funnel, a single Shopping campaign pays the same for weak and strong keywords, and Google tends to route search terms into the campaign with the highest bid. The funnel's priority and negative keyword setup prevents this. [L0742.006]
- **Older (2021-22), setting:** New standard Shopping campaigns default to *Campaign priority: Low (default)*, so every copy must be changed by hand. Open the campaign's Settings, set Campaign priority to High, Medium or Low, and click Save. [L0742.035]

**Priority and campaign roles (three-campaign funnel, older 2021-22):**

| Campaign priority | Search intent served | Bid level | Bid given in the source | Negative lists applied (per L0742.028) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| High | Low value, generic terms | Low | Not stated | Master Generic, Brand Names, Product Ids |
| Medium | Medium value, branded medium-value terms | Medium | 60 cents | Master Generic, Product Ids |
| Low | High value, terms with a product-specific identifier | High | About $1.20 | Master Generic |

*Conflict:* Procedure step 9 of the build sequence also applies Brand Names to the Medium campaign, while the setting and mistake units say Brand Names belongs on the High priority campaign only. The table follows the setting and mistake units. [L0744.005, L0742.007, L0742.028, L0742.029]

- **Older (2021-22):** In a three-campaign Shopping funnel, the high priority campaign with low bids targets low-value generic terms. The medium priority campaign with medium bids targets branded medium-value terms. The low priority campaign with high bids targets high-value terms that contain a product-specific identifier. [L0744.005]
- **Older (2021-22):** The store's own brand name is a valuable search term, because shoppers already know the store and have a high chance of converting. Such terms belong in the high-value campaign. [L0744.039]

  *Conflict:* L0744.005 places branded medium-value terms in the Medium campaign, while L0744.039 places the store's own brand name in the high-value campaign. Both apply: the store's own brand name goes to the high-value campaign, and branded medium-value terms go to the Medium campaign.

### Building the three-campaign funnel

- **Older (2021-22):** For a high-ticket dropshipping store, build a Google Shopping funnel of at least three campaigns. Three is the standard starting point, and four to six are rarely needed, since most accounts need only three. [L0742.001]
- **Older (2021-22):** Each campaign in the funnel targets one search intent level: low value (generic terms, lowest bids), medium value (more specific or brand-plus-category terms, middle bids) and high value (terms naming one exact product, highest bids). Separate campaigns make it possible to bid differently per value level instead of paying the same for weak and strong keywords. [L0742.002]
- **Older (2021-22):** Campaigns must be identical (same ad groups, product groups and products) except for priority, bids and negative keyword lists. Duplicating a campaign is the fastest way to build the other two. [L0742.032]
- **Older (2021-22):** Some Google Shopping funnels have been built with up to nine campaigns, but for about 90% of high-ticket dropshipping cases three campaigns are enough. Add a fourth or fifth campaign only when the account clearly needs it. [L0742.045]
- **Older (2021-22):** The shopping funnel requires a very precise campaign setup. If it is not configured exactly as described, it will not work and will not produce the intended results. [L0740.019]
- **Older (2021-22):** The shopping funnel gives control over two things: which search terms the ads show for, and how much is paid per click based on search intent. This control is the reason the structure exists. [L0740.018]
- **Older (2021-22):** Set up the Google Shopping campaigns in a three-tier structure and add a trademark search text ad campaign for the brand name. [L1145.045]
- **Older (2021-22):** A three-campaign setup keeps paid traffic in separate campaigns, such as branded search, Shopping and display remarketing. Each stage can then be measured and budgeted on its own. [L0719.044]

#### Build procedure

**Older (2021-22), procedure:** Build the three-campaign Google Shopping funnel in this order:

1. Create the first Shopping campaign in the Google Ads account, choose Standard Shopping (not Smart Shopping) and select the Merchant Center account and the country of sale.
2. Enter the campaign name, choose Manual CPC bidding, apply the shared budget from the shared library, and set campaign priority.
3. Set Targeting: keep Search Network, optionally with YouTube, Gmail and Discover; do not include Google search partners.
4. Create the first ad group (product shopping type, named by brand), enter a starting CPC bid, and save.
5. In product groups, subdivide by the Custom label 1 brand label, then save without editing bids; exclude "Everything else in All products".
6. Subdivide further by the Custom label holding product titles, select all products, and save without editing bids.
7. Duplicate the campaign with Edit > Copy and Paste, rename each copy (High, Medium, Low), and set its campaign priority.
8. Set bids per campaign: Medium campaign at 60 cents, Low priority campaign at about $1.20, and apply negative keyword lists.
9. Apply Master Generic negatives to all three campaigns, Brand Names negatives to the High priority campaign only (and to the Medium campaign, see below), and Product Ids negatives to the High and Medium priority campaigns.
10. Enable all paused campaigns once products are approved in Merchant Center.

[L0742.007]

- **Older (2021-22), procedure:** Subdivide product groups as follows: first subdivide by the custom label holding the brand name, then subdivide by the custom label holding the product title. Do not use the default item ID because it shows an unreadable string. Select all products, click Save without editing bids, then change bids on individual products as needed. [L0742.024]
- **Older (2021-22):** Two custom labels are needed in Merchant Center or the product feed: one holding the brand name and one holding the product title as shown on the store. Subdividing product groups by these labels gives readable names, which the default item ID grouping does not. [L0742.046]
- **Older (2021-22):** Every new product added to the store needs its custom labels added manually in the product feed. Without them, the product does not populate into the ad group and product group segmentations. [L0744.041]
- **Older (2021-22):** When new products or brands are added, the product ID list or brand name list used for negative keyword and campaign separation must be updated. Otherwise their search terms land in the high priority campaign at a low bid and lose out on high-value terms. [L0744.040]

### Negative keyword lists

- **Older (2021-22):** Negative keywords are central to the Shopping funnel because they let you shape campaigns around search terms of different value. Creating the lists is part of setup, and using them to manage campaigns is an ongoing task after launch. [L1074.005]
- **Older (2021-22), mistake:** Using negative keywords incorrectly stops the Shopping funnel from working effectively. List setup and later changes to them need care. [L1074.006]
- **Older (2021-22):** Negative keyword lists are the mechanism that tells Google which search terms to push between the three campaigns. Each term must be blocked from the campaigns that should not serve it. [L0742.030]
- **Older (2021-22):** Negative keyword lists tell Google which campaign a search term may appear in. This keeps each term in its correct campaign and keeps the priority structure working. Without them, low-value terms leak into high-bid campaigns. [L0744.006]
- **Older (2021-22), rule:** The three lists have distinct roles:
  - *Master Generic Negatives* holds search terms that the products should never match in any campaign.
  - *Brand Names* holds the names of the brands the store sells, so branded searches are pushed past the lowest-bid campaign.
  - *Product Ids* holds the product identifiers, so exact product searches are pushed to the highest-bid campaign.

  [L0742.041]
- **Older (2021-22), setting:** Negative keyword list assignment for the funnel: Master Generic Negatives applied to all three campaigns. Brand Names applied to the High priority campaign only, because search terms with brand names move past the lowest-bid campaign. Product Ids applied to the High and Medium priority campaigns, because very specific product terms move to the Low priority, highest-bid campaign. [L0742.028]
- **Older (2021-22), mistake:** The Brand Names negative list was wrongly applied to two campaigns. It must be applied only to the High priority campaign, so check each negative list's campaign assignments after applying. [L0742.029]
- Google Shopping chooses the search terms unless you exclude them, so traffic is shaped with negative keywords rather than long-tail targeting. On search text ads, more specific long-tail terms usually raise CTR and lower traffic. [L0879.032]
- **Older (2021-22):** Google does not reliably judge search intent and often shows ads for loosely related searches. Leaving these matches unreviewed burns budget. Review which search terms trigger the ads and exclude the poor ones with negative keywords. [L0739.017]
- **Older (2022):** The beta campaign also needs strong negative terms such as brand names and SKU numbers, while the alpha campaign only needs the universal negatives. [L1113.054]
- Block descriptive search terms that convert well but are not brand-specific as negatives in both Alpha and Beta. Then raise CPC in Beta and check whether higher-quality traffic comes in. Do not create a third campaign for this at the start. [L0472.002]

### Brand names and the two-campaign alternative (Source A)

- Searches for a brand name convert well, because the shopper already knows the brand. Example: *Lifestyles infrared sauna* converts higher than *infrared sauna* or *should I buy this*, because generic searchers are earlier in the funnel doing comparison shopping. [L0225.006]
- Source A's account structure separates Alpha and Beta, and the bids differ by query type. **Procedure (undated):** To segment a Shopping campaign into a branded and a generic campaign:
  1. Open the account and click the edit button, then copy and paste the existing product listing ad campaign so you have two campaigns.
  2. In the generic campaign, go to the Keywords tab, click Keywords, and add negative phrase keywords for your brand terms (brand name, brand possessive, model names) so only generic queries trigger it.
  3. In the branded campaign, add negative exact keywords for the generic terms (for example *sunglasses* and *men's sunglasses*) so only branded queries trigger it.
  4. Set low bids in the generic campaign and high bids in the branded campaign.

  [L1328.008]
- Blocking low-converting generic terms completely gives up profitable traffic. Keep them in a separate generic campaign with a low bid instead, where they can remain ROI positive. [L1328.010]
- **Two-campaign vs. three-campaign:** Source A's segmentation uses two campaigns (branded and generic). Source B's funnel uses three priority levels and states that three campaigns are standard for most high-ticket cases. The sources do not state which to use in which case; the three-campaign funnel is the standard the older source sets for high-ticket dropshipping. [L1328.008, L0742.001, L0742.045]

### Alpha and Beta campaigns (Source A)

- A Google Ads account for e-commerce is organised in two layers: campaign stage (MOFU or BOFU) and campaign type. Each campaign should be placed in one stage and one type so the structure stays readable. [L0867.001]
- Build Google Ads campaigns bottom-up: start with BoFU audiences (ready to buy). Avoid spending on TOFU (awareness-only) as the entry point, then expand upward to MOFU and TOFU once BoFU revenue scales. [L0023.003]
- Search terms that convert well in Shopping campaigns are the money terms. They are moved into their own cold-traffic Search campaign, so budget and bids can be controlled for proven keywords. [L0867.003]
